OR-2026R1-HB4016.s: Public contractors would have to show and keep up to date on tax compliance before a public contract can be signed. It also directs the Secretary of State to study ways to use the state business registry to help make sure businesses are tax compliant. The law takes effect June 5, 2026, and the new contractor rule becomes operative January 1, 2027.

OR-2026R1-HB4018.s: Changes several election and campaign finance rules, including timing for new rules, committee names, in-kind gifts, money that can be carried over, and filing deadlines. It also lets corporations and labor unions set up separate funds that work like political committees, and it allows some election law violations to be fixed after the fact. The measure became law and took effect on passage, because it declares an emergency.

OR-2026R1-HB4020.s: Certain state agencies would have to say what legal authority they used to deny a permit and give the applicant a guide on how to challenge that denial. They would also have to create a way to track how quickly permit and permit renewal requests are handled. The bill became law and takes effect on June 5, 2026.

OR-2026R1-HB4021.s: Changes the timing and notice rules for some permanent agency rules that are adopted, changed, or ended. It also requires certain agencies to post contact information on their websites so people can ask questions about each rule. The law takes effect on the 91st day after lawmakers adjourn, which is June 5, 2026.

OR-2026R1-HB4027.s: The law changes how the Bureau of Labor and Industries is funded. It creates a new fund for bureau costs, raises a fee limit tied to some public works contracts, and requires a study and reports on labor agency funding and bureau staffing needs. It was signed into law and takes effect June 5, 2026.

OR-2026R1-HB4033.s: The bill moves the ORVID volunteer database from the Higher Education Coordinating Commission to the Oregon Department of Emergency Management. The department would update and keep the database going. It passed and took effect on passage as an emergency law.

OR-2026R1-HB4036.s: Creates a fund to help preserve affordable housing that is at risk of being lost. It lets the state issue $100 million in bonds for the 2025-2027 budget period and directs the housing agency to report on barriers to building affordable housing by December 1, 2026. The law took effect on April 7, 2026.

OR-2026R1-HB4037.s: Oregon law changes some housing rules for cities, counties, state agencies, landlords, and tenants. It changes a loan program for affordable housing, sets a faster plan review limit for homes with two or fewer units, and creates a local process for some housing approvals using clear and objective standards. It also sets rules for housing after natural disasters, gives housing providers priority for some surplus state property, and takes effect on June 5, 2026, with some parts operative on July 1, 2026.

OR-2026R1-HB4040.s: The law makes many changes to health care, insurance, and medical licensing rules in Oregon. It changes some hospital screening and medical assistance rules, sets new rules for some insurance claims and coverage, and updates several state health care boards and programs. It also changes who can serve in some care roles and who may qualify for certain licenses or license status. It was signed into law and took effect on April 7, 2026.

OR-2026R1-HB4043.s: The measure lets the State Treasurer issue state bonds to pay for renovating or expanding courthouses. It also requires the local mental health program director to tell the court within two judicial days if a defendant found unfit to stand trial is not following community treatment rules, and lets that duty be handed to the service provider. It became law and takes effect on January 1, 2027.

OR-2026R1-HB4052.s: Creates a corporate excise tax credit for the first three years that an Oregon-chartered bank does business in the state. The credit would apply to banks that start business in tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2027, and before January 1, 2033. It became law and takes effect on June 5, 2026.

OR-2026R1-HB4057.s: Oregon lawmakers passed a bill that requires the Department of Early Learning and Care to give people applying for, or waiting for, the Employment Related Day Care subsidy program standard information about publicly funded early learning and child care programs and resources in the state. The department can let the Department of Human Services provide that information instead. It also asks for a review of background check rules for some publicly funded staff and a report by September 15, 2026.

OR-2026R1-HB4061.s: The law directs the Oregon Business Development Department to create a grant program for small businesses to help with higher costs from federal tariffs. It also calls for updates to Oregon’s trade plan, a procurement reform roadmap from the Department of Administrative Services by December 15, 2026, and a task force to make business retention recommendations. It passed and took effect on March 31, 2026.

OR-2026R1-HB4062.s: The law requires the director of the Oregon Business Development Department to review the department’s programs and suggest ways to make them simpler. It also declares an emergency, so it took effect when it was passed. It affects the department’s programs and the people who run them or use them.

OR-2026R1-HB4065.s: The bill changes rules for late payments on seed production contracts and seed purchase contracts for farm seed and other seed. It was passed and became law. It took effect on March 31, 2026.

OR-2026R1-HB4066.s: The law makes several changes to Oregon education rules. It limits how the student member of the Oregon Health and Science University board can take part in talks about student collective bargaining, sets a rule that the board must meet at least four times a year, lets education service district board members get stipends, and changes some state education duties and reports. It also lets some school districts and education service districts use new exceptions in a few cases, and it took effect on March 31, 2026 as an emergency law.

OR-2026R1-HB4069.s: Requires employers of behavioral health workers to have a written safety policy or plan to protect the physical safety of those workers. It applies to behavioral health employers in Oregon. The law takes effect on July 1, 2027.

OR-2026R1-HB4070.s: The law changes Oregon's medical assistance program and behavioral health services. It requires the state health agency and care groups to make behavioral health care access similar to medical and surgical care, and it updates rules for some telemedicine pay. It also clarifies some service roles and duties. The law takes effect June 5, 2026, and parts of it become operative on January 1, 2027.

OR-2026R1-HB4072.s: The law changes the deadline for arraignment, which is the first court appearance after an arrest, for people released from custody. It excludes certain time periods from the count for when that arraignment must happen. It became law and takes effect on June 5, 2026.

OR-2026R1-HB4075.s: The bill lets the State Treasurer use up to $44 million from the Unclaimed Property and Estates Fund to back a loan for a rural hospital so it can stabilize its finances. It affects a rural hospital that gets this loan support. It became law and took effect on April 7, 2026.

OR-2026R1-HB4076.s: This law changes how some energy projects can move forward in Oregon. It lets state and local officials make exceptions to some land-use rules for certain renewable energy facilities or other energy facilities that use unused or surplus connections to the power grid and do not need new transmission lines more than two miles long. It takes effect on June 5, 2026.

OR-2026R1-HB4084.s: Oregon’s legislature passed a law that creates a Joint Permitting Council to run a fast-track permit program for economic development projects. It also tells some state agencies to publish a list of permits they issue, within 120 days after the law takes effect. The law also changes parts of the enterprise zone program, limits its use for data centers, and changes some job tax credits; it takes effect on June 5, 2026.

OR-2026R1-HB4089.s: Oregon's law changes theft of services to include partial payments and says a theft case does not stop other legal action. It also tells a state network to look at possible theft of services cases and possible tax and labor law problems. The law raises penalties for some acts tied to unlicensed labor contractors and for misuse of a contractor license number, and it takes effect January 1, 2027.

OR-2026R1-HB4100.s: Bulk oil and fuel terminal owners or operators would have to get a financial responsibility certificate from the Oregon Department of Environmental Quality. The state would set rules for those certificates, and the department would report on how the law is working every two years. Local governments could not require extra financial backing beyond what the law says. It has been signed into law and took effect on March 31, 2026.

OR-2026R1-HB4108.s: Allows the City of Eugene to annex land that is not next to the city if all landowners petition for it and the land meets four set rules. It applies only to land in Eugene. The law takes effect on January 1, 2027.

OR-2026R1-HB4111.s: The law bars a person’s immigration status from being used as evidence in a civil case, with some exceptions. It also makes it unlawful for employers to punish or treat workers badly because they update personal information after a lawful change in work papers. It also adds immigration status to the rules on law enforcement profiling, and it takes effect on June 5, 2026.

OR-2026R1-HB4114.s: Oregon HB 4114 would let people sue certain federal or out-of-state law enforcement agents if they enter certain property without a warrant or a valid exception. It would also require notice and ID from those agents before planned operations in Oregon, and it would limit state and local police from working with agents who do not follow those rules or who target certain sensitive places without permission. The bill was signed into law and declares an emergency, so it took effect on passage.

OR-2026R1-HB4115.s: The law changes some background check rules for certain caregivers and behavioral health providers. It makes some criminal records checks last for three years, lets some valid checks carry over to other care settings, and says when a new background check is needed. It also requires certain health plans to pay some behavioral health providers back to the date they first applied to enroll, and bars those plans from making them file a new credentialing application when they change employers. It takes effect on June 5, 2026.

OR-2026R1-HB4121.s: Oregon’s emergency management law would create new state offices and powers to help coordinate emergency planning. It would also set new duties for state agencies, change rules for Resilience Hubs and Networks, allow some training sites to hold overnight training, and set up grant programs for emergencies. The law also requires fingerprint checks for some employees and contractors, lets counties waive some food facility fines during emergencies, and takes effect on January 1, 2027.

OR-2026R1-HB4123.s: Limits when a landlord can share private information about a renter. It also lets people seek set cash damages if a landlord knowingly breaks these rules. The law takes effect June 5, 2026.

OR-2026R1-HB4124.s: Passed law in Oregon and took effect on March 31, 2026. It directs the Higher Education Coordinating Commission to study the state post-secondary education system and make detailed recommendations for how it should be organized and run. The commission must send a preliminary report by October 1, 2026, and a final report by April 1, 2027, to legislative committees on higher education.

OR-2026R1-HB4130.s: The bill lets land under processing facilities qualify for a special property tax break. It also explains what counts as "preparing" farm products or by-products for people or animals under the farm use rules. The law takes effect on January 1, 2027.

OR-2026R1-HB4131.s: The law directs the State Board of Pharmacy to license qualified applicants to run a mobile pharmacy, which is a pharmacy that travels from place to place. It also sets rules for how a mobile pharmacy must operate. It took effect on June 5, 2026.

OR-2026R1-HB4132.s: The law changes how Oregon supports veterans. It sets a goal of at least $10 million a year for the veterans affairs department, adds staff roles, and creates a Veterans Employment Coordinator. It also starts a grant program for suicide prevention and job training, raises the cap on one education grant from $5,000 to $10,000, and takes effect July 1, 2026.

OR-2026R1-HB4134.s: The law raises Oregon’s state hotel and short-term lodging tax. It also renames a wildlife fund account and sets how the extra money from the tax increase will be shared. The higher tax applies to lodging charges on or after January 1, 2027, and the law took effect on June 5, 2026.

OR-2026R1-HB4138.s: The law requires law enforcement officers to wear uniforms with certain ID details, with some exceptions, and limits when officers can wear face coverings. It also bars employees of state and local law enforcement and some other public bodies from taking part in certain actions, and tells agencies to adopt policies to match. Volunteers in a civil defense force are treated as agents of a public body for state tort claim rules, and a person hurt by certain violations can ask a court to stop them. It took effect on passage and became law on March 31, 2026.

OR-2026R1-HB4140.s: Changes Oregon rules for scrap metal and metal theft. It would add new rules for selling certain nonferrous and commercial metal to scrap metal businesses, require some sellers to register with the Department of Justice, and require scrap metal businesses to check ownership and seller registration and use a theft alert system. It also changes the crime of first-degree criminal mischief for some telecommunications property. The law was signed and takes effect January 1, 2027.

OR-2026R1-HB4142.s: The law expands who can qualify for medical marijuana use. It also requires some organizations and residential facilities that act as extra caregivers to make written rules and train staff, but it exempts hospitals and hospital-linked clinics. Patients or residents must be medical marijuana cardholders or have applied for a card, and nurses cannot be disciplined for talking with patients about medical marijuana. It was signed into law and takes effect on June 5, 2026.

OR-2026R1-HB4144.s: The law requires battery makers and makers of products with batteries to join a producer group and set up a program to collect and recycle batteries. It gives the Oregon Department of Environmental Quality the job of enforcing the rules and creates a fund for the program. It also allows civil penalties for breaking the law. The law takes effect January 1, 2027.

OR-2026R1-HB4148.s: Passed law would change how local hotel and lodging tax money can be spent. It would let cities and counties use some of that money for grants to small restaurants and lodging businesses, and it would set the split at 50 percent for tourism-related costs and 50 percent for city or county services. It would also require local governments to report how they use this tax money every two years, and the law takes effect on June 5, 2026.

OR-2026R1-HB4149.s: Requires school districts to adopt rules so homeless students can enroll right away, be placed in school, and get needed services. It also tells the state education department to name a coordinator for homeless student education. The law takes effect on January 1, 2027.

OR-2026R1-HB4151.s: The bill would raise penalties for making a false report that causes a bigger police response and leads to serious injury or death. A person could face up to five years in prison, a $125,000 fine, or both. It takes effect on January 1, 2027.

OR-2026R1-HB4153.s: The law lets counties approve farm stores as a nonfarm use on land zoned for farming. It affects county land-use decisions and farmers who may want to use farm land for these stores. It was signed into law and takes effect on January 1, 2027.

OR-2026R1-HB4154.s: The law requires schools to compile data on students who attend regularly or are chronically absent. It takes effect July 1, 2026. It was signed into law on March 31, 2026, and the emergency clause made it effective on passage.

OR-2026R1-HB4156.s: The law changes the rules for extra Medicaid payments to emergency medical services providers. It took effect on passage, and the law was signed on March 31, 2026.

OR-2026R1-HB4162.s: The law repeals Measure 119, which had required some Oregon cannabis license holders to sign labor peace agreements with unions that represent their workers. It affects certain businesses licensed by the Oregon Liquor and Cannabis Commission. The law takes effect on January 1, 2027.

OR-2026R1-HB4177.s: The bill would update Oregon rules for public meetings. It would change how notices, minutes, and recordings are handled, and it would make clear that meetings may be in person, online, or both. It would also change the complaint process and the training and penalty rules for public meetings law.

OR-2026R1-HB4179.s: The bill lets Oregon Health and Science University create and keep a nonprofit corporation under state law, as long as the university is a corporate member. It says certain people who give patient care for that nonprofit are acting as part of their state job duties, and it treats the group as a public employer under the state union law. It also says some rules for professional corporations do not apply to the group. The law takes effect on January 1, 2027.

OR-2026R1-HB5203.s: Approves some new or higher fees set by state agencies. It applies to state financial matters and took effect on passage as an emergency measure. It became law on April 7, 2026.

OR-2026R1-HB5204.s: The bill changes how state money is set aside for some Oregon agencies and the Emergency Board for the next two-year budget period. It also changes spending limits for some of those agencies. It became law and took effect on passage, on April 7, 2026.

OR-2026R1-SB1501.s: The measure lets the Oregon Department of Administrative Services make agreements to own and oversee the Moda Center in Portland. It creates a special state fund for this and sends certain tax money tied to work in and around the arena into that fund. The agreements cannot use state money outside that fund, and the law took effect on March 31, 2026.

OR-2026R1-SB1502.s: The bill directs the Secretary of State to file a proposal before the 2027 regular session. That proposal would lay out the secretary’s suggested changes to the state’s campaign finance limits. It became law and takes effect on June 5, 2026.

OR-2026R1-SB1507.s: This law changes several Oregon tax rules, including income tax credits and some business tax rules. It raises the earned income tax credit, ends some federal tax breaks for Oregon taxes, and creates a tax credit for employers that add new jobs. Some changes start for tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2026, and the law takes effect on June 5, 2026.

OR-2026R1-SB1509.s: Sets rules for who can serve as an elector for President and Vice President in Oregon and what must go in the paper that names the electors. It says an elector who does not vote as pledged loses the office, and it gives a way to fill that opening. Electors who attend the meeting and cast a valid ballot can get mileage pay. It takes effect on July 1, 2026.

OR-2026R1-SB1510.s: Changes several Oregon tax rules. It updates some income tax terms for multinational companies, extends or lines up end dates for some tax credits and exemptions, expands a film tax credit to cover commercials, and makes other tax admin changes for some taxpayers and tax preparers. It takes effect on June 5, 2026, and some parts apply later to tax years starting in 2026 or 2027.

OR-2026R1-SB1515.s: The bill changes rules for seeking money after a wrongful conviction. It also creates a new way to ask for post-conviction relief when a conviction was based on certain scientific expert testimony or evidence from discredited forensic fields. The new process ends on January 2, 2031, and the law took effect on April 7, 2026.

OR-2026R1-SB1516.s: The law expands the crime of aggravated harassment to cover threats against public officials in some cases and allows penalties of up to five years in prison, a fine of up to $125,000, or both. It also limits how police can use automated license plate readers, how long they can keep the data, and when they can share it. The law changes some rules for pretrial release orders and the Justice Reinvestment Equity Program, and it took effect on March 31, 2026.

OR-2026R1-SB1517.s: The law lets an operator of a sport, fitness, or recreation activity ask people to sign away claims for ordinary carelessness in some cases. It also says some claims cannot be waived, and that a court must decide whether a risk was part of the activity. It became law right away because it declared an emergency.

OR-2026R1-SB1519.s: The law changes how workers’ compensation is figured for total disability. It uses a new formula for both temporary and permanent total disability pay, based on whether a worker’s wage is at or below 75% of the state average weekly wage or above it. It takes effect on January 1, 2027.

OR-2026R1-SB1521.s: The law limits when cities and counties in the Portland metro area can require developers to include affordable homes in multiunit buildings. Before making that rule, they must first figure out the developers' average expected losses and make up those losses. It takes effect for rental housing on January 1, 2028, and for all housing on January 1, 2029.

OR-2026R1-SB1525.s: Creates a Blue Economy Task Force to study Oregon’s blue economy and report its findings to the Legislature by September 15, 2027. It also lets the Oregon Ocean Science Trust create and keep a nonprofit group. The law takes effect on June 5, 2026.

OR-2026R1-SB1533.s: The law changes the Oregon Foster Children's Bill of Rights and the sibling rights law for foster children. It also adds a rule for abuse cases when the suspected abuser is the child’s parent, and it requires the Department of Human Services to tell parents or guardians that its staff are not their lawyer and cannot give legal advice. It became law on March 31, 2026, and was made an emergency measure.

OR-2026R1-SB1535.s: The law requires the Department of Early Learning and Care to study child care and report its findings to lawmakers by September 15, 2027. It also lets the Early Learning Council change priority for some families in the Employment Related Day Care subsidy program, which helps pay for child care. The department must also lead a work group to study liability insurance and other liability issues for child care providers and report options to lawmakers by November 1, 2027. It became law and takes effect June 5, 2026.

OR-2026R1-SB1539.s: Allows a person to check whether cattle are pregnant without a veterinary license in some cases. It also lets the Oregon State Department of Agriculture make rules for this. The law takes effect on January 1, 2027 and ends on January 1, 2031.

OR-2026R1-SB1544.s: The measure changes several transportation rules in Oregon. It would require the Transportation Department to report on an audit, new design practices, a transportation university, and a new data base, and it would direct the Transportation Director to bring project work under one plan. It also would end the Joint Committee on Transportation, change rules for dismantlers, and expand who can qualify for public transportation funding. It was signed into law and takes effect June 5, 2026.

OR-2026R1-SB1546.s: The law requires AI companion services to tell users they are talking with computer-made output when a reasonable person might think they are talking with a real person. It also requires safety steps for signs of suicidal thoughts or self-harm, extra notices for minors, and a yearly public report on those incidents. People who are harmed can sue for money damages or a court order. It takes effect January 1, 2027.

OR-2026R1-SB1565.s: The law increases snowmobile registration fees. It took effect on June 5, 2026, and affects snowmobile owners who register their machines in Oregon.

OR-2026R1-SB1570.s: The bill would set rules for hospitals and federally qualified health centers on how they handle a person's immigration status and country of birth as private health information. It would limit sharing that information with law enforcement unless state or federal law or a court order requires it, and it would require hospitals to have plans for law enforcement visits. It would also bar retaliation against workers who share materials about immigration rights and legal services, and it was signed into law with an effective date of June 5, 2026.

OR-2026R1-SB1571.s: This law changes Oregon rules for nicotine and tobacco products, including inhalant delivery systems like vaping devices. It replaces the criminal ban on selling these products to people under 21 with a civil rule handled by the Oregon Health Authority, which can fine people for violations. It also bans giving these products away for free and says sales of these products must happen in person at licensed stores. The law takes effect on June 5, 2026.

OR-2026R1-SB1575.s: The law adds new rules for getting an initial license to run a hospice program, and a hospice must apply for a new license if ownership changes. It also bars people excluded from Medicare or Medicaid, or found liable for fraud or abuse, from having an ownership stake in a hospice program. The Oregon Health Authority must write the rules within 24 months, and most new hospice licenses cannot be issued until that is done; it took effect on April 7, 2026.

OR-2026R1-SB1576.s: Requires state building rules to match federal fair housing access rules and certain housing access standards. It also bars the Housing and Community Services Department from funding new subsidized rental housing unless it meets set accessibility standards. The law takes effect June 5, 2026.

OR-2026R1-SB1585.s: The bill sets the highest local match that small incorporated cities must provide to get certain state grants for capital projects and city infrastructure improvements. It takes effect on June 5, 2026.

OR-2026R1-SB1587.s: Oregon public bodies would be barred from giving a data broker personal information unless the broker says it will not be sold or passed on to anyone who would use it to enforce federal immigration law. The rule would not apply when the law already requires the release, when a court orders it, or when the information is shared on the same terms as it is available to the public. It became law and takes effect June 5, 2026.

OR-2026R1-SB1590.s: This law prohibits public bodies from helping the federal government privatize certain federally owned lands. It took effect on March 31, 2026, and it sunsets on January 2, 2032. An emergency was declared, so it became law right away.

OR-2026R1-SB1595.s: A professional licensing board would have to publish guidance about licensure and make sure some staff get training on working with people from different cultures by January 1, 2028. It also declares an emergency, so it took effect when signed. The bill became law in Oregon.

OR-2026R1-SB1598.s: The law requires some health plans to cover preventive care under federal rules in place on June 30, 2025, and future vaccines recommended by the state Public Health Officer. It also lets the Public Health Officer, or a doctor they choose, issue a standing order for a prescription to help control, prevent, or treat certain diseases or other major public health concerns. The law took effect on March 31, 2026.

OR-2026R1-SB1601.s: Oregon would change several state finance and reporting rules. It would fix an internal legal reference, extend a deadline for sex offender classification, change reporting for summer learning grants, and remove references to monthly pay for some state officials. It would also allow certain money to be used for PCB testing, move some money to the General Fund, direct some transportation funds to operations and maintenance, and remove the cap on lottery money sent to the County Fair Account. It became law and took effect on April 7, 2026.

OR-2026R1-SB5701.s: This law changes how much debt the state can issue for the two-year budget period. It also allows bonds and participation certificates for Moda Center improvements, updates some lottery bond rules, and authorizes more lottery bonds. It sets extra requirements for the Oregon State University Cascades Student Health and Recreation Center project and took effect on passage.

OR-2026R1-SB5702.s: The law changes how some state agencies can pay for capital construction from certain funds. It also extends the end dates for some approved construction projects and spending limits. It took effect on April 7, 2026.

OR-2026R1-SB5703.s: Sets two-year state budget limits and spending levels for the biennium ending June 30, 2027. It also changes how money is split from several state funds, including funds for economic development, veterans' services, criminal fines, marijuana revenue, and student success. The law took effect on April 7, 2026.
